Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. The first Russian composer to achieve international renown, writing some of the most popular and emotionally expressive works of the Romantic era.

While his contemporary nationalist peers in Russia, known as the Mighty Handful, rejected Western conservatory training, Tchaikovsky combined traditional Russian folk song with Western European symphonic forms. His music is characterized by its rich, sweeping melodies and deep, often tragic, emotional weight.

His Symphony No. 6 in B minor was nicknamed Pathétique by his brother Modest. It was his final completed work, premiering just nine days before his death. Unusually, it concludes with a slow, despairing Adagio lamentoso that fades into silence rather than a triumphant finale. The second movement is in a dancing, asymmetrical five-four time signature.

The 1812 Overture is a bombastic programmatic work commemorating Russia's defense against Napoleon's invasion. It is famous for incorporating live cannon fire, brass fanfares, and cathedral bells to represent the Russian victory over the French.

Romeo and Juliet is a fantasy-overture based on Shakespeare's tragedy, structured in sonata form. It contains one of the most famous Love Themes in classical music.

The Violin Concerto in D major is one of the pillars of the violin repertoire. It was initially declared unplayable by the dedicatee Leopold Auer before being championed by Adolph Brodsky.

The Piano Concerto No. 1 in B-flat minor is famous for the grand, sweeping horn calls and string theme that open the first movement.

Tchaikovsky is universally famous for his canonical ballets. Swan Lake represents his early breakthrough. The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker followed. The Nutcracker is famous for introducing the celesta to depict the Sugar Plum Fairy. These three works are the cornerstones of classical dance.

Nadezhda von Meck was a wealthy widow who supported Tchaikovsky financially for thirteen years. She allowed him to compose full-time, on the strict condition that they never meet in person.

Tchaikovsky's personal life was marked by depression and isolation, exacerbated by the necessity of hiding his homosexuality in imperial Russia. This led to a disastrous, short-lived marriage to Antonina Miliukova, which caused him a nervous breakdown. His sudden death at age fifty-three was officially attributed to cholera contracted from drinking unboiled water, though some historians suspect it was suicide, possibly forced by a court of honor threatening to expose his sexuality.
